summary: Explains why mass unsolicited email and postings, known as spam, are harmful to the Internet community, and gives guidelines for avoiding it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a polite reminder not to mail the same advert to thousands of strangers, because it clogs mailboxes and makes people cross.

subtitle: Why mass unsolicited email harms the Internet and how to handle it.

tldr.problem: Mass unsolicited email and newsgroup postings, called spam, consume recipients' bandwidth and storage, harm the Internet's viability as a communications medium, and shift costs from spammers to victims.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains why spam is harmful from economic, technical, and ethical perspectives, then provides guidelines for users, administrators, and ISPs to recognize, report, and prevent spam.
tldr.outcome: Spam remains a growing problem, but the document establishes best practices for responding to spam without worsening the situation, such as reporting to postmasters rather than responding directly.

facts.label: Spammer email advantage
facts.value: Four orders of magnitude cheaper than paper mail

facts.label: Remove request risk
facts.value: Over 80% chance of increased spam in tests

today: RFC 2635 remains informational guidance on spam handling from 1999. Spam continues to grow, though modern techniques like DKIM, SPF, and machine learning filters offer better defenses than were available when this RFC was written.

sections.title: What Is Spam
sections.content:
The term spam refers to mass unsolicited electronic mail messages or newsgroup postings sent to many recipients without their consent. The word comes from a Monty Python sketch where the word "spam" overwhelms every item on a menu, mimicking how spam overwhelms communication channels with unwanted messages.

The problem is compounded because users often send angry replies to mailing lists or newsgroups asking to be removed, creating a cascade of unwanted traffic far larger than the original message. Some newsgroups use automated cancelbots to delete spam, but the cancel messages themselves now generate as much traffic as the spam they are meant to prevent.
sections.eli5: Spam is junk mail sent to lots of people at once through email or newsgroups. The problem is that when people try to complain or unsubscribe, they create even more junk mail.

sections.title: Why Mass Mailing Is Harmful
sections.content:
In paper mail, senders pay most of the cost, so there is a built-in incentive to mail only to interested recipients. Electronic mail inverts this: recipients bear the majority of the cost in connectivity charges and disk storage. Bulk electronic mail costs spammers about 1/100th of a cent per address—four orders of magnitude cheaper than paper mail.

This cost imbalance has serious consequences. Without incentive to maintain quality mailing lists, spammers send to indiscriminate addresses. The resulting volume threatens the Internet's viability: entire mail services regularly collapse from spam overload, forcing providers to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars upgrading equipment, costs passed to customers.

Most responsible Internet citizens regard unsolicited mass mail as a form of theft of service, since the recipient must pay for delivery and storage of the spammer's message. Beyond the technical harm, the RFC argues that this is fundamentally an ethical issue: senders should ask themselves whether they would accept receiving 90%, 95%, or 99% advertisements.
sections.eli5: When you get junk postal mail, the sender paid to mail it. But with email, you pay to receive it. This makes spam extremely cheap for spammers but expensive for everyone else.

sections.title: Responding to Spam
sections.content:
For users receiving spam, the safest response is simply to delete it. Other options include using email filters, contacting a local postmaster with headers, or using the abuse.net service. However, the RFC strongly advises against using the "remove" option in unsolicited email: tests show that replying to unsubscribe requests actually increases future spam by confirming the address is valid. Responding directly to the sender often fails anyway because spammers forge their headers to hide their true location.

For system administrators, best practices include configuring mail servers to reject open relay usage, using firewalls to restrict unwanted NNTP access, and requiring email headers to comply with standards like RFC 822. Setting clear policies and providing filter rules helps users handle unwanted mail locally. Administrators can also block persistent offending sites, though care must be taken not to block legitimate mail.

The RFC includes detailed guidance on reading mail headers to identify the true source of spam, tracing routes with whois and traceroute, and contacting the responsible ISP with full header information.
sections.eli5: If you get spam, the best thing is to delete it. Do not click "unsubscribe" because it tells spammers your email works. Instead, tell your postmaster (the person who runs your email system) about it.

sections.title: ISP and Provider Responsibilities
sections.content:
ISPs should adopt a clear policy on unsolicited mail and publish an Acceptable Use Policy that states consequences for violations, including account termination. Providers must ensure mail servers are configured securely to prevent relay abuse, limit dialup accounts from sending bulk mail, and maintain current, audited mail software.

ISPs should establish an abuse@domain mailbox that is monitored and handled by someone with authority to investigate and stop abuses. The RFC recommends following RFC 2142 for mailbox naming conventions. ISPs should educate users about mail filtering and, most importantly, educate themselves about spam so they can work with law enforcement when necessary and pursue civil actions against spammers for damages to their network.

The RFC notes that spammers sometimes forge headers or bounce mail through open servers and dial-up accounts, so providers should exercise caution and courtesy when investigating, recognizing that the apparent originating site may itself be a victim.
sections.eli5: Email providers should have a clear rule against spam, have a way for people to report it, and be ready to shut down the spammer's account if needed.

sections.title: Identifying and Tracing Spam
sections.content:
The RFC includes a practical appendix explaining how to read mail headers and identify the true source of spam, since spammers frequently forge the visible sender information. The most reliable parts of a header are those added by systems under control of the recipient's mail server, particularly the Received: headers that show the path a message took.

Techniques for tracing spam include using whois to find who administers a domain and traceroute to identify the path to an IP address. If spam advertises a web site, that site must be connected to the network to be usable, making it a valid complaint target for the ISP hosting it. The RFC cautions that the advertised site might itself be a victim of an attack using it as a target.

In Usenet news, spammers exploit open news servers and remailers; header forgery is common. The document includes an example mail header with detailed annotation to illustrate how to identify routing and source information.
sections.eli5: Email headers show the path a message traveled. By reading them carefully, you can find where the spam really came from, even if the sender's name is fake.
